heuristic: When TC or the reference level drifts, tune the reference-generation block first (bias distribution and temperature-dependent element operating points), and only then touch the regulation/amplifier loop, because the reference core typically dominates both TC and the achieved Vref window.

If PSR is the limiting metric, first reduce supply-to-bias feedthrough inside the reference-generation biasing/mirroring (e.g., by increasing bias-source stiffness and local isolation), then re-center Vref afterward to avoid solving PSR by inadvertently shifting the reference operating point.

When improving PSR, treat loop-gain investment as a power tradeoff: strengthen the main signal-path small-signal authority over the control/bias node before increasing overall biasing, and after each change verify the power objective still improves under the same PSR check.

To reduce TC without excessive power, adjust the biasing of the temperature-sensing/diode-connected elements to move their operating region (and therefore their temperature coefficients) rather than simply increasing overall current levels; then re-validate power since the same bias knobs commonly move both metrics.

Once constraints are met, minimize power by backing off global bias currents in coordinated steps while watching PSR and TC simultaneously, because power shows repeated coupling to both PSR and TC and single-metric reductions can silently degrade either.

Because PSR and TC show recurring tradeoff behavior, lock an acceptable TC margin before pursuing aggressive PSR improvements, and reject PSR changes that require compensatory TC fixes in a different block unless the net system margin increases.

If power is unexpectedly high after Vref regulation is correct, audit the startup-assist path to ensure it fully self-disables in steady state and does not continue to load the main bias/control node; only after leakage is controlled should you tune core biases for further power savings.

For PSR tuning, split effort between the reference-generation bias network and the main signal path (rather than pushing one block to extremes), and iterate with small cross-checks, since both roles repeatedly show significant influence on PSR.

When Vref (or any secondary reference node) is within limits but PSR/TC are not, avoid “fixes” that move the reference level first; instead improve rejection and temperature behavior at the existing operating point, then re-check that Vref and Vref2 remain inside bounds as a guardrail.

Establish loop stability first by shaping the dominant compensation dynamics (dominant pole/zero placement and effective compensation strength), and only then tune speed (lg_ugb, rise_time) and secondary margins (cmpm), because the compensation function consistently exerts the strongest leverage on these metrics.

When both differential-mode stability (pm) and common-mode stability (cmpm) are constrained, co-design the compensation and common-mode control dynamics as a coupled problem (adjust them in small alternating steps and re-verify both margins together), since repeated evidence shows a tradeoff between pm and cmpm rather than independent improvement.

If rms_noise_out is limiting while minimizing power, prioritize reducing noise at the dominant signal-path contributors (where input-referred noise is set) and treat any bias/current re-allocation as a deliberate power–noise exchange, since repeated results show power and rms_noise_out trade off.

When pushing bandwidth (lg_ugb) under a tight noise ceiling (rms_noise_out), plan for an explicit bandwidth–noise trade space: adjust the speed-setting mechanisms (including compensation-related dynamics) while continually re-checking noise, because repeated evidence shows lg_ugb and rms_noise_out trade off.

Do not rely on compensation adjustments as the primary lever for rms_noise_out; instead, first meet pm/rise_time with compensation, then attack rms_noise_out through the main signal path, because compensation shows strong influence on stability/speed but only weak influence on output noise in this case.

When simultaneously targeting high adm and high cmrr, avoid optimizing either in isolation; enforce balanced symmetry/matching and consistent impedance levels across the differential paths, and iterate with both metrics measured each step, since repeated evidence indicates an adm–cmrr tradeoff.

If psrr and/or cmrr are weak, focus on increasing isolation from supply/common-mode disturbances at the main gain-generating nodes (e.g., by raising effective impedances and reducing disturbance coupling paths) while re-checking stability and speed, since the main signal path shows measurable (though weaker) coupling into psrr/cmrr.

Treat rise_time as a stability-linked speed metric: once pm is safely met, adjust compensation to recover rise_time without eroding pm, and re-verify after each change because the same compensation mechanisms significantly affect both rise_time and pm.

For late-stage closure when most DC specs are already satisfied, use compensation-centric fine-tuning to trim pm/lg_ugb/cmpm/rise_time margins (with frequent re-simulation), because these metrics respond strongly to compensation changes while DC gain/rejection metrics tend to be less directly sensitive.

If the output level is outside its allowed window, first correct the DC feedback scaling in the feedback network (setpoint path) and re-validate vout_min/vout_max before changing biasing, output drive, or compensation; this isolates setpoint errors from loop-dynamics tuning and avoids chasing the wrong knob.

When minimizing power, treat PSRR as a co-equal guardrail: reduce static drive and bias only after PSRR is comfortably above the minimum, and after each power-saving change re-check PSRR (and not just DC regulation), since the history shows power and PSRR can move in opposition.

If lowering power starts to erode the lower bound of the regulated output, back off the power-reduction lever that reduces available control headroom (e.g., weakens the ability to fully enhance the output device) and restore margin before continuing; power and vout_min exhibited coupled movement, so maintain output headroom first, then resume power optimization.

When line_regulation is poor or PSRR is marginal, prioritize reducing supply sensitivity in the main signal path and biasing (improving intrinsic rejection and loop gain against supply variation) before tuning the output stage for power; verify line_regulation and psrr together because they can trade off and improvements in one can conceal degradation in the other.

Optimize load_regulation and line_regulation as a coupled pair: after any change that improves one, immediately re-check the other and adjust loop aggressiveness (effective loop gain/bandwidth vs. output drive authority) to balance both, since the dataset indicates a recurring tradeoff between them.

If improving PSRR worsens load_regulation (or vice versa), add or preserve control authority where the loop moves the output actuator (driver strength and ability to move the control node quickly) while keeping high-frequency supply feedthrough limited; sequence as: secure DC setpoint, then balance load_regulation vs psrr, then revisit power.

When multiple specs fluctuate unpredictably despite a correct nominal output, suspect loop-shaping/compensation interactions: adjust compensation/feedforward to separate the dominant regulation behavior from high-frequency ripple coupling, and only then re-optimize gain/drive; this avoids mistaking instability or excess peaking for true regulation or PSRR limits.

To reduce power without breaking regulation, preserve sufficient small-signal gain in the error/control path (the part that senses the feedback error) before trimming the output stage; cut power in places that do not directly reduce error-path gain, then confirm both load_regulation and line_regulation remain bounded.

Use a staged optimization order that matches observed dominance: (1) lock vout_min/vout_max via the feedback network, (2) tune line_regulation and load_regulation via error-path gain and control authority while watching their tradeoff, (3) finally push power down while continuously guarding psrr; this sequencing reflects which roles most strongly moved each metric in the run history.
Prefer the Bias network role when targeting slew_rate_rise or slew_rate_fall because adjusting Idc is the strongest first lever.
Prefer the Main signal path role when noise remains limiting because input-pair/load sizing is the strongest first lever.
Increasing Idc (not Idc2 or Idc3) can improve slew rates.
Increase w of input pair and decrease w of load at constant Idc can improve noise with slew rates unchanged.
Prefer the Main signal path role when targeting adm because gain is mainly set by the telescopic core gm*ro through the input pair, cascodes, and active load.
Increasing lengths of the cascodes and active load, and increasing input-pair gm at controlled current, can improve adm.
